latin: Non ergo ideo aduersus nos insaniunt, quia dii non coluntur a nobis — a multis enim non coluntur — sed quia ueritas penes nos est, quae, ut est uerissime dictum, odium parit. quid igitur existimabimus nisi nescire illos quid patiantur? pergitur enim caeco et inrationabili furore, quem nos uidemus, illi nesciunt. non enim ipsi homines persecuntur, qui causam cur irascantur innocentibus non habent, sed illi spiritus contaminati ac perditi, quibus ueritas et nota est et inuisa, insinuant se mentibus eorum et instigant nescios in furorem. hi enim, quamdiu pax est in populo dei, fugitant iustos et pauent, et cum corpora hominum occupant animasque diuexant, adiurantur ab iis et nomine dei ueri fugantur. quo audito tremunt et exclamant et uri se uerberarique testantur et interrogati qui sint, quando uenerint, quomodo in hominem inrepserint, confitentur. sic extorti et excruciati uirtute diuini nominis exulantur. propter haec uerbera et minas sanctos et iustos uiros semper oderunt. et quia per se nocere iis nihil possunt, publicis eos odiis persecuntur, quos sibi graues sentiunt, exercentque saeuitiam quam uiolentissime possunt, ut aut eorum fidem minuant per dolorem aut, si id efficere non quiuerint, auferant omnino de terra, ne sint qui possint eorum nequitiam coercere.

non me fugit quid responderi e contrario possit: \'cur ergo deus ille singularis, ille magnus, quem rerum potentem, quem dominum omnium confiteris, haec fieri patitur nec cultores suos aut uindicat aut tuetur? cur denique qui eum non colunt, et opulenti et potentes et beati sunt et honoribus regnoque potiuntur eosque ipsos dicioni suae ac potestati sub- iectos habent?\' reddenda et huius rei ratio est, ne quid remaneat erroris. nam in primis haec causa est cur existimetur religio dei uim non habere, quod inducuntur homines specie terrenorum ac praesentium bonorum, quae ad curam mentis nullo modo pertinent. quibus quia carere iustos uident et afluere iniustos, et dei cultum inanem arbitrantur, in quo inesse illa non cernunt, et deorum ritus aestimant ueros, quoniam cultores eorum et diuitiis et honoribus et regnis fruantur.

uerum ii qui sunt in hac existimatione non perspiciunt altius uim rationemque hominis, quae tota non in corpore, sed in mente est. nihil enim uident amplius quam (quod oculis? uidetur, corpus scilicet. quod quia oculis manuque tractabile est, inbecillum fragile mortale est: cuius sunt illa omnia bona quae cupiditati ac miraculo sunt, opes honores imperia, quoniam corpori adferunt uoluptates, et ideo tam caduca sunt quam corpus ipsum. animus uero, in quo solo est homo, quoniam subiectus oculis non est, nec bona eius aspici possunt, quae in sola uirtute sunt posita, et ideo tam stabilis et constans et perpetuus sit necesse est sicut ipsa uirtus, in qua est animi bonum.

author: Lactantius
english: Sometimes, however, they sense that they are evil, and they praise the condition of the old ages, and from their own manners and deserts they conjecture that justice is absent: which, though it stands before their eyes, they not only do not take up or recognize, but even violently hate and persecute and strive to wipe out. Let us suppose for a moment that this which we follow is not justice: how, if that comes which they think true, will they receive it—they who tear and kill those whom they themselves confess to be imitators of the just, because they do good and just works? How much more, when they kill the pious and count the very followers of justice as enemies—indeed more than enemies? This is beyond telling which is done against those who do not know how to do evil, and none are held more harmful than those who are of all the most innocent. Dare then the most wicked men make mention of justice—men who surpass wild beasts in savagery, who lay waste the most peaceful flock of God like ravening wolves?

What shall we say is the chief cause of this so great and so stubborn hatred? Is it that truth begets hatred, as the poet says as if inspired by a divine spirit, or that they blush to be worthless in the presence of the just and good, or rather both? For truth is always hated for this reason: that the one who sins wants to have a free place for sinning, and thinks he can enjoy the pleasure of evil deeds more securely in no other way than if there is no one to whom crimes are not pleasing. Therefore, as witnesses of their crimes and malice, they strive to root them out utterly and remove them, and they think them heavy to themselves, as if their life were being convicted. Why should there be some unseasonably good, who by living well put a reproach on public morals corrupted? Why should not all be equally evil—rapacious, shameless, adulterers, perjurers, greedy, fraudulent? Rather let those be taken away before whom it is shameful to live badly, who strike and scourge the brow of sinners, if not with words—because they are silent—yet by the very unlike manner of life. For whoever disagrees seems to chastise. Nor is it greatly to be wondered if these things are done against humans, when even the people established in hope and not ignorant of God rose against God himself for the same cause, and the same necessity follows the just which violated the author of justice himself.

They therefore vex and by exquisite kinds of punishments torture, and think it too little to kill those they hate unless cruelty also mocks the bodies. But if any, by fear of pain or death or by their own treachery, have deserted the heavenly sacrament and consented to deadly sacrifices, they praise them and load them with honors, that by their example they may entice the rest. But those who have prized faith highly and have not denied that they are worshipers of God—against these they throw the whole strength of their butchery, as if they thirst for blood, and they call them desperate because they spare their own body so little: as if anything could be more desperate than to torture and tear the one you know to be innocent. But what of these can be charged against our people, whose whole religion is to live without crime and without stain? Since then they see themselves and theirs doing the things we have said, and ours doing nothing else than what is fair and good, they could, if they had any sense, from this understand both that those who do good are pious and that they themselves are impious who commit unspeakable things. For it cannot be that those who do not err in all the acts of their life should err in the very sum, that is in religion, which is the head of all things: for impiety taken up in that which is highest would follow through all the rest. Equally it cannot be that those who themselves err in every life should not also be deceived in religion, since piety holding the rule in the highest would keep its course in the rest. So it comes about that on either side, from the condition of the things that are done, what the sum itself is may be known.

latin: Nonnumquam tamen sentiunt se malos esse et ueterum saeculorum statum laudant et de suis moribus meritisque coniectant abesse iustitiam: quam obuersantem oculis suis non tantum non suscipiunt nec adgnoscunt, uerum etiam uiolenter oderunt et persecuntur et exterminare contendunt. fingamus hanc interim non esse iustitiam quam nos sequimur: quomodo si illa uenerit quam ueram putant, eam recipient? qui laniant et occidunt eos quos et ipsi fatentur imitatores esse iustorum, quia bona operentur et iusta, cum si tantummodo malos occiderent, digni essent ad quos iustitia non ueniret: cui nulla fuit alia causa linquendi terram quam humani cruoris effusio. quanto magis, cum pios interficiant et ipsos iustitiae sectatores pro hostibus ducant, immo uero plus quam pro hostibus? quibus utique, cum animas eorum et opes et liberos ferro et igni adpetant, tamen parcitur uictis et est locus inter arma clementiae, aut si adeo saeuiri placuit, nihil plus in eos fit quam ut occidantur uel in seruitutem abducantur. hoc uero inenarrabile est quod fit aduersus eos qui malefacere nesciunt, et nulli nocentiores habentur quam qui sunt ex omnibus innocentes. audent igitur homines inprobissimi iustitiae facere mentionem, qui feras inmanitate uincunt, qui placidissimum dei gregem uastant lupi ceu raptores atra in nebula, quos inproba uentris exegit caecos rabies . uerum hos non uentris, sed cordis rabies efferauit nec atra in nebula, sed aperta praedatione grassantur nec eos umquam conscientia scelerum reuocat, ne sanctum ac pium nomen iustitiae ore illo uiolent quod cruore innocentium tamquam rictus bestiarum madet.

huius tanti et tam pertinacis odii quam potissimum causam esse dicamus? utrumne ueritas odium parit, ut ait poeta quasi diuino spiritu instinctus, an erubescunt coram iustis et bonis esse nequam, an potius utrumque? nam et ueritas ideo semper inuisa est, quod is qui peccat uult habere liberum peccandi locum nec aliter se putat malefactorum uoluptate securius perfrui posse, quam si nemo sit cui delicta non placeant. ergo tamquam scelerum et malitiae suae testes extirpare funditus nituntur et tollere grauesque sibi putant, tamquam uita eorum coarguatur. cur enim sint aliqui intempestiue boni, qui corruptis moribus publicis conuicium bene uiuendo faciant? cur non omnes sint aeque mali rapaces inpudici adulteri periuri cupidi fraudulenti? quin potius auferantur quibus coram male uiuere pudet, qui peccantium frontem etsi non uerbis, quia tacent, tamen ipso uitae genere dissimili feriunt et uerberant. castigare enim uidetur quicumque dissentit. nec est magnopere mirandum, si aduersus homines ista hunt, cum aduersus ipsum deum propter eandem causam insurrexerit etiam populus in spe constitutus nec dei nescius, sequiturque iustos eadem necessitas quae ipsum iustitiae uiolauit auctorem.

uexant ergo et exquisitis poenarum generibus excruciant parumque habent interficere quos oderunt, nisi etiam crudelitas corporibus inludat. si qui autem doloris uel mortis metu uel suapte perfidia caeleste sacramentum deseruerint et ad funesta sacrificia consenserint, eos laudant et honoribus mact.ant, ut eorum exemplo ceteros inliciant. qui autem magni aestimauerint fidem cultoresque se dei non abnegauerint, in eos uero totis carnificinae suae uiribus, ueluti sanguinem sitiant, incumbunt et desperatos uocant, quia corpori suo minime parcunt: quasi quicquam desperatius esse possit quam torquere ac dilaniare eum quem scias esse innocentem. adeo nec pudor ullus aput eos superest a quibus abest omnis humanitas et retorquent in homines iustos conuicia sibi congruentia. inpios enim uocant, ipsi scilicet pii et ab humano sanguine abhorrentes, cum si et actus suos considerent et illorum quos tamquam inpios damnant, iam intellegant quam mendaces sint et iis omnibus quae aduersus bonos aut dicunt aut faciunt digniores. non enim de nostro, sed ex illorum numero semper existunt qui uias obsideant armati, maria praedentur, uel si palam grassari non licuit, uenena clam temperent, qui uxores necent, ut dotes earum lucrentur, aut maritos, ut adulteris nubant, qui natos ex se pueros aut strangulent aut, si nimium pii fuerint, exponant, qui libidines incestas nec a filia nec sorore nec: matre nec sacerdote contineant, qui aduersus ciues suos patriamque coniurent, qui nec culleum metuant, qui denique sacrilegia committant et deorum quos colunt templa despolient, et, ut quae levia sunt atque usitata dicamus, qui hereditates captent, testamenta supponant, iustos heredes uel auferant uel excludant, qui corpora sua libidinibus prostituant, qui demque inmemores quid nati sint, cum feminis patientia certent, qui sanctissimam quoque corporis sui partem contra fas omne polluant ac profanent, qui uirilia sua ferro metant et, quod est sceleratius, ut sint religionis antistites, qui ne uitae quidem suae parcant, sed extinguendas publice animas suas uendant, qui si iudices sedeant, aut inmeritos perdant mercede corrupti aut noxios inpune dimittant, qui caelum quoque ipsum ueneficiis adpetant, tamquam illorum malitiam terra non capiat: haec, inquam, et his plura scelera utique ab iis fiunt qui deos colunt. quis inter haec tot et tanta iustitiae locus est? et ego de multis pauca collegi, non ut arguerem, sed ut ostenderem. qui uolet scire omnia, Senecae libros in manum sumat, qui morum uitiorumque publicorum et descriptor uerissimus et insectator acerrimus fuit. sed et Lucilius tenebrosam istam uitam circumscripte breuiterque depinxit his uersibus: nunc uero a mani ad noctem, festo atque profesto, totus item pariterque die populusque patresque iactare indu foro se omnes, decedere nusquam, uni se atque eidem studio omnes dedere et arti, uerba dare ut caute possint, pugnare dolose; blanditia certare, bonum simulare uirum se; insidias facere, ut si hostes sint omnibus omnes . nostro autem populo quid horum potest obici, cuius omnis religio est sine scelere ac sine macula uiuere? cum igitur uideant se ac suos ea quae diximus gerere, nostros autem nihil aliut operari nisi aecum et bonum, poterant, si quid saperent, ex hoc intellegere et illos qui bonum faciunt pios esse et se inpios qui nefanda committunt. neque enim fieri potest ut : qui in omnibus uitae suae actibus non errant, in ipsa summa errent, hoc est in religione, quae rerum omnium caput est: inpietas enim suscepta in eo quod est summum per cetera uniuersa sequeretur. aeque fieri non potest ut ipsi qui errant in omni uita, non et in religione fallantur, quoniam pietas in summo regulam tenens tenorem suum seruaret in ceteris. ita fit ut in utraque parte de condicione rerum quae geruntur qualis sit summa ipsa noscatur.

author: Lactantius
english: But since our number is always increased from the worshipers of the gods, and is never lessened even in the persecution itself — because humans can sin and be defiled by sacrifice, but cannot be turned away from God: for truth is strong by its own force — who at last is so senseless and so blind that he does not see on which side wisdom is? But they are blinded by malice and fury, that they may not see, and they think those foolish who, though they have it in their power to avoid punishments, prefer nonetheless to be tortured and to die, though from this very fact they could perceive that that is not folly into which so many thousands of humans throughout the whole world agree with one and the same mind. If women slip by the weakness of their sex — for sometimes they call this a womanish or old-womanish superstition — men at least are wise. If boys and youths are improvident by age, the mature and the old at least have stable judgment. If one city is mad, the rest beyond number cannot be foolish. If one province or one nation lacks prudence, all the others must have understanding of what is right. But when from the rising of the sun even to its setting the divine law has been taken up, and every sex, every age and people and region serves God with one and equal minds, and there is the same patience everywhere, the same contempt of death, they ought to have understood that there is something of reason in that matter which is defended not without cause even unto death, something of foundation and solidity which not only does not dissolve that religion by injuries and vexation, but always increases it and makes it firmer.

For in this too their malice is convicted: that they think they have overturned God's religion from the foundation if they have defiled humans, though both it is allowed to make satisfaction to God, and there is no worshiper of God so bad that, when opportunity is given, he does not return to appeasing God, and indeed with greater devotion. For conscience of sin and fear of punishment makes one more religious, and the faith that penitence puts back is always much firmer. If therefore they themselves, when they think the gods angry at them, still believe them to be appeased by gifts and sacrifices and incense, why at last do they think our God so harsh, so implacable, that he who has poured a libation to their gods under compulsion and unwillingly should seem already unable to be a Christian? Unless perhaps they think that those once contaminated will transfer their mind so that they begin of their own will to do what they did through torments. Who would willingly take up that service which began from injury? Who, when he sees the scars of his sides, would not rather hate the gods for whose sake he bears everlasting marks of punishments and brands pressed into his flesh? So it happens that when peace is given from heaven, both all who fled return and another new people is added because of the miracle of virtue. For when the crowd sees humans torn by various kinds of torments and, among worn-out executioners, holding an unconquered patience, they judge — which is the fact — that neither the consent of so many nor the perseverance of those dying is empty, nor that patience itself can overcome such great tortures without God. Robbers and men of strong body cannot endure lacerations of that kind: they cry out and give groans, for they are conquered by pain, because inspired patience is absent from them. But ours — to say nothing of men — boys and weak women silently conquer their torturers, and not even fire can wring a groan from them.

This is true virtue, which the philosophers too, glorying, toss about not in deed but in empty words, discoursing that nothing so befits the gravity and constancy of a wise man as that he cannot be driven by any terrors from his opinion and purpose, but that it is worth so much to be tortured and to die, lest he betray faith, lest he depart from duty, lest, subdued by fear of death or bitter pain, he do anything unjust — unless perhaps Flaccus seems to them to rave in his lyrics when he says that the just man, tenacious of purpose, is not shaken in solid mind by the citizens' heat ordering what is crooked, nor by the face of the pressing tyrant. Nothing truer can be said, if this is referred to those who refuse no tortures, no death, lest they decline from faith and justice, who do not tremble at tyrannical orders or the swords of governors so as not to defend with constant mind true and solid freedom, which in this alone is to be guarded by the wise. For who is so insolent, so lifted up, that he forbids me to lift my eyes to heaven, that he lays on me the necessity either of worshiping what I do not will or of not worshiping what I will? What further is left to us, if even this which ought to be done by will alien lust wrings out? No one will accomplish that, if we have any virtue for despising death and pain. If we hold that constancy, why are we judged fools for doing the things the philosophers praise? Rightly therefore Seneca, objecting incongruity to humans, says: the highest virtue seems to them a great mind, and yet the same people hold him who despises death for a madman — which is certainly of the highest perversity. But these worshipers of empty religions object that by the same folly by which they do not understand the true God: whom the Erythraean Sibyl calls deaf and senseless, who neither hear divine things nor perceive them, but fear and adore earth imagined by their own fingers.

latin: Cum autem noster numerus semper de deorum cultoribus augeatur, numquam uero, ne in ipsa quidem persecutione minuatur — quoniam peccare homines et inquinari sacrificio possunt, auerti autem non possunt a deo: ualet enim ui sua ueritas — quis est tandem tam excors tamque caecus quin uideat in utra sit parte sapientia? sed illi malitia et furore caecantur, ne uideant, stultosque esse arbitrantur qui cum habeant in potestate supplicia uitare, cruciari tamen et emori malunt, cum possint ex eo ipso peruidere non esse stultitiam in quam tanta hominum milia per orbem totum una et pari mente consentiant. si enim feminae sexus innrmitate labuntur - nam interdum isti muliebrem aut anilem superstitionem uocant — uiri certe sapiunt. si pueri, si adulescentes inprouidi sunt per aetatem, maturi certe ac senes habent stabile iudicium. si una ciuitas desipit, ceterae utique innumerabiles stultae esse non possunt. si una prouincia, una natio prudentia caret, ceteras omnes habere intellegentiam recti necesse est. cum uero ab ortu solis usque ad occasum lei diuina suscepta sit et omnis sexus, omnis aetas et gens et regio unis ac paribus animis deo seruiat, eadem sit ubique patientia, idem contemtus mortis, intellegere debuerant aliquid in ea re esse rationis quod non sine causa usque ad mortem defendatur, aliquid fundamenti ac soliditatis quod eam religionem non tantum iniuriis et uexatione non soluat, sed augeat semper et faciat firmiorem.

nam et in hoc quoque illorum malitia conuincitur, quod euertisse se funditus religionem dei opinantur, si homines inquinauerint, cum et deo satisfacere liceat et nullus sit tam malus dei cultor quin data facultate ad placandum deum reuertatur et quidem deuotione maiore. peccati enim conscientia et metus poenae religiosiorem facit et semper multo firmior est fides quam reponit paenitentia. si ergo ipsi cum deos sibi arbitrantur iratos, tamen donis et sacrificiis et odoribus placari eos credunt, quid est tandem cur deum nostrum tam inmitem, tam inplacabilem putent, ut uideatur is iam Christianus esse non posse qui diis eorum coactus inuitusque libarit? nisi forte contaminatos semel putant animum translaturos, ut sua sponte iam facere incipiant quod per tormenta fecerunt. quis id officium libens obeat quod ab iniuria coepit? quis cum uideat laterum suorum cicatrices, non magis oderit deos, propter quos aeterna poenarum insignia et inpressas uisceribus suis notas gestet? ita fit ut data diuinitus pace et qui fugerunt uniuersi redeant et alius propter miraculum uirtutis nouus populus accedat. nam cum uideat uulgus dilacerari homines uariis tormentorum generibus et inter fatigatos carnifices inuictam tenere patientiam, existimant, id quod res est, nec consensum tam multorum nec perseuerantiam morientium uanam esse nec ipsam patientiam sine deo cruciatus tantos posse superare. latrones et robusti corporis uiri eiusmodi lacerationes perferre non queunt, exclamant et gemitus edunt, uincuntur enim dolore, quia deest illis inspirata patientia: nostri autem, ut de uiris taceam, pueri et mulierculae tortores suos taciti uincunt et exprimere illis gemitum nec ignis potest. eant Romani et Mucio glorientur aut Regulo, quorum alter necandum se hostibus tradidit, quod captiuum puduit uiuere, alter ab hostibus deprehensus cum uideret mortem se uitare non posse, manum foco iniecit, ut pro facinore suo satisfaceret hosti quem uoluit occidere, eaque poena ueniam quam non meruerat accepit: ecce sexus infirmus et fragilis aetas dilacerari se toto corpore urique perpetitur non necessitate, quia licet uitare si uelint, sed uoluntate, quia confidunt deo.

haec est uera uirtus, quam philosophi quoque gloriabundi non re, sed uerbis inanibus iactant disserentes nihil esse tam congruens uiri sapientis grauitati atque constantiae quam nullis terroribus de sententia et proposito posse depelli, sed tanti esse cruciari et emori, ne fidem prodat, ne ab officio discedat, ne metu mortis aut dolore acerbo subactus aliquid faciat iniustum: nisi forte delirare illis uidetur Flaccus in lyricis, cum dicit: iustum et tenacem propositi uirum non ciuium ardor praua iubentium, uon uultus instantis tyranni mente quatit solida. quo nihil uerius dici potest, si hoc ad eos referatur qui nullos, cruciatus, nullam mortem recusant, ne a fide iustitiaque declinent, qui non tyrannicas iussiones, non praesidum gladios tremunt, quominus ueram et solidam libertatem constanti mente defendant, quae in hoc solo tuenda sapienti est. quis enim tam insolens, tam elatus est qui me uetet oculos in caelum tollere, qui inponat mihi necessitatem uel colendi quod nolim uel quod uelim non colendi? quid iam nobis ulterius relinquatur, si etiam hoc quod uoluntate fieri oportet libido extorqueat aliena? nemo istut efficiet, si quid nobis ad contemnendam mortem doloremque uirtutis est. quam constantiam si tenemus, cur stulti iudicamur facientes ea quae philosophi laudant? recte igitur Seneca incongruentiam hominibus obiectans ait: summa uirtus illis uidetur magnus animus, et idem eum qui contemnit mortem pro furioso habent: quod est utique summae peruersitatis. sed hi uanarum religionum cultores eadem stultitia id obiciunt qua uerum deum non intellegunt: quos Sibylla Erythraea xuxpoy ? et avoTQVOj ; uocat, surdos scilicet et excordes, qui nec audiant diuina nec sentiant, sed terram digitis suis imaginatam metuant et adorent.

author: Lactantius
english: It would be long to bring forward all the kinds of virtue, that I may teach concerning each how necessary it is that the wise and just man be far estranged from those goods: by enjoying which, because the unjust enjoy them, the worship of the gods is believed true and effective. For the present question it is enough if from one virtue we prove what we intend. Certainly patience is a great and chief virtue, which alike the public voices of the crowd and the philosophers and the orators celebrate with highest praises. And if it cannot be denied that it is the highest virtue, it is necessary that the just and wise man be in the power of an unjust human, so that he may take on patience. For patience is the enduring with even mind of evils which are either inflicted or befall. Therefore the just and wise man, because he takes on virtue, has patience in himself: which he will wholly lack if he suffers nothing adverse. On the contrary, he who lives in prosperous things is impatient and lacks the greatest virtue: I call him impatient because he suffers nothing. He also cannot keep innocence, which itself is a virtue proper to the just and wise man, but he both harms often and desires what is another's and seizes by wrong what he has desired, because, empty of virtue, he is subject to vice and sin and, forgetful of frailty, swells with a mind insolently lifted. Hence the unjust and those who do not know God flourish in riches and power and honors. For all these are the rewards of injustice, because they both cannot be perpetual and are sought through desire and violence. But the just and wise man, because he judges all those human things — as Laelius said — his goods divine, desires nothing of another's, lest he hurt anyone at all against the right of humanity, nor desires any power or honor, lest he do injury to anyone — for he knows that all, generated by the same God and under the same condition, are joined by the right of brotherhood — but content with his own and with little, because mindful of his frailty, he seeks no more than whence to sustain life, and from that itself which he has had he also imparts to the one who has not, because he is pious; and piety is the highest virtue. Besides, he despises fleeting and vicious pleasures, for whose sake wealth is sought, since he is continent and conqueror of lusts. The same, bearing no swelling and insolence, does not lift himself higher nor raise a proud head, but is calm and agreeing and common and level, because he knows his condition. Since therefore he does injury to none nor desires what is another's nor even defends his own if they are taken by force, since he knows how to bear even an inflicted injury moderately, because he is endowed with virtue, it is necessary that the just human be subject to the unjust and that the wise be afflicted with insults by the foolish, so that both that one may sin, because he is unjust, and this one may have virtue in himself, because he is just.

But if anyone wants to know more fully why God allows the evil and unjust to become powerful, blessed, rich, and on the contrary suffers the pious to be lowly, wretched, poor, let him take up that book of Seneca whose title is 'Why many evils befall good men, though there is providence.' In which he has spoken many things not plainly by secular ignorance, but wisely and almost divinely. God, he says, holds humans as children, but he suffers the corrupt and vicious to live luxuriously and softly, because he does not think them worthy of his correction. But the good, whom he loves, he chastens more often and by continual labors trains for the use of virtue, nor does he allow them to be corrupted and depraved by fleeting and mortal goods. Whence it ought to seem wonderful to no one if for our faults we are often chastened by God. Indeed when we are vexed and pressed, then most of all we give thanks to the most indulgent Father, because he does not suffer our corruption to proceed further, but corrects by blows and stripes. From which we understand that we are a care to God, at whom, since we sin, he is angry. For though he could bestow both wealth and kingdoms on his people as he had given before to the Jews, whose successors and posterity we are, for that reason he willed that people to live under another's sway and command, lest corrupted by the happiness of prosperous things it should slide into luxury and despise God's precepts as those ancestors of ours did, who often, enervated by these earthly and fragile goods, wandered from discipline and broke the bonds of the law. He therefore provided how far he would grant rest to his worshipers if they had kept the commands, and yet would correct them if they had not obeyed the precepts. And so, lest they be corrupted by leisure as much as their fathers by license, he willed them to be pressed by those in whose hands he placed them, that he may both strengthen those slipping and restore the corrupted to fortitude and test and prove the faithful. For how can a commander prove the virtue of his soldiers unless he has had an enemy? And yet for that one an adversary rises against his will, because he is mortal and can be conquered; but for God, because he cannot be resisted, he himself raises up adversaries to his name, not who fight against God himself, but against his soldiers, that he may either prove or confirm the devotion and faith of his own, until by the blows of pressure he corrects dissolving discipline.

There is also another cause why he allows persecutions to be made against us, that God's people may be increased: nor is it hard to show why or how that happens. First many are driven from the cults of the gods by hatred of cruelty: for who would not shudder at such sacrifices? Next virtue itself and faith please some. Some suspect that the cult of the gods is not without cause thought evil by so many humans, that they prefer to die rather than do that which others do in order to live. Someone desires to know what that good is which is defended even unto death, which is preferred to all things that are pleasant and dear in this life, from which neither loss of goods nor of light nor pain of body nor torments of the vitals deter. These avail very much, but those causes especially have always increased our number: the surrounding people hears amid the very torments those saying that they do not sacrifice to stones made by human hand, but to the living God who is in heaven. Many understand this to be true and admit it into the breast. Then, as usually happens in uncertain matters, while they ask among themselves in turn what the cause of this perseverance is, many things that pertain to religion, published and caught by rumor in turn, are learned: which, because they are good, must please. Besides, the vengeance that followed, as always happens, drives strongly to believing. Nor is this a light cause either: that unclean spirits of demons, when license is received, plunge themselves into the bodies of many, from whom afterward, when they have been cast out, all who have been restored cling to the religion whose power they have felt. These so many causes gathered into one acquire a great multitude for God in a wonderful way.

latin: Longum est uniuersas uirtutis species promere, ut de singulis doceam, quam necesse sit sapientem ac iustum uirum longe ab illis bonis abhorrere: quibus quia fruuntur iniusti, deorum cultus ueri et efficaces esse creduntur. quod ad praesentem pertinet quaestionem, satis est si ex una uirtute id probemus quod intendimus. nempe magna et praecipua uirtus est patientia, quam pariter et uulgi publicae uoces et philosophi et oratores summis laudibus celebrant. quodsi negari non potest quin summa sit uirtus, necesse est iustum et sapientem uirum in potestate esse hominis iniusti, ut capiat patientiam. patientia est enim malorum quae aut inferuntur aut accidunt cum aequanimitate perlatio. ergo iustus ac sapiens quia uirtutem capit, habet in se patientiam: qua carebit omnino, si nihil patietur aduersi. contra qui in rebus prosperis agit, inpatiens est et uirtute maxima caret: inpatientem dico, quia nihil patitur. innocentiam quoque seruare non potest, quae et ipsa iusto et sapienti uiro propria uirtus est, sed et nocet saepe et concupiscit aliena et rapit quae cupierit per iniuriam, quia uirtutis expers uitio peccatoque subiectus est et fragilitatis oblitus animo insolenter elato tumet. inde iniusti ac deum nescientes et diuitiis et potentia et honoribus florent. haec enim cuncta iniustitiae praemia sunt, quia et perpetua esse non possunt et per cupiditatem uiolentiamque quaeruntur. iustus uero ac sapiens quia illa omnia humana, ut est a Laelio dictum, sua bona diuina iudicat, nec alienum quicquam concupiscit, ne quem contra ius humanitatis laedat omnino, nec ullam potentiam honoremue desiderat, ne cui faciat iniuriam — scit enim cunctos ab eodem deo et eadem condi- cione generatos iure fraternitatis esse coniunctos —, sed et suo contentus et paruo, quia fragilitatis suae memor, non amplius quaerit quam unde uitam sustentet, et ex eo ipso quod habuerit inpertit etiam non habenti, quia pius est; pietas autem summa uirtus est. accedit quod uoluptates caducas uitiosasque contemnit, quarum causa opes adpetuntur, quoniam continens est ac libidinum uictor. idem nihil tumoris atque insolentiae gerens non extollit se altius nec erigit superbum caput, sed placidus et concors et communis et planus est, quia condicionem suam nouit. cum ergo iniuriam nulli faciat nec aliena cupiat nec sua quoque si ui auferantur defendat, cum sciat etiam inlatam iniuriam moderate ferre, quia uirtute praeditus est, necesse est iustum hominem subiectum esse iniusto et contumeliis adfici ab insipiente sapientem, ut et ille peccet, quia iniustus est, et hic in se uirtutem habeat, quia iustus est

si quis autem uolet scire plenius cur malos et iniustos deus potentes beatos diuites fieri sinat, pios contra humiles miseros inopes esse patiatur, sumat eum Senecae librum cui titulus est \'Quare bonis uiris multa mala accidant, cum sit prouidentia\'. in quo ille multa non plane inperitia saeculari, sed sapienter ac paene diuinitus elocutus est. deus inquit homines pro liberis habet, sed corruptos et uitiosos luxuriose ac delicate patitur uiuere, quia non putat emendatione sua dignos. bonos autem, quos diligit, castigat saepius et adsiduis laboribus ad usum uirtutis exercet nec eos caducis ac mortalibus bonis conrumpi ac deprauari sinit. unde nemini debet mirum uideri si pro nostris saepe delictis castigamur a deo. immo uero cum uexamur ac premimur, tum maxime gratias agimus indulgentissimo patri, quod corruptelam nostram non patitur longius procedere, sed plagis ac uerberibus emendat. ex quo intellegimus esse nos deo curae, quibus, quoniam peccamus, irascitur. nam cum posset populo suo et opes et regna largiri sicut dederat ante Iudaeis, quorum nos successores ac posteri sumus, idcirco eum uoluit sub aliena dicione atque imperio degere, ne rerum prosperarum felicitate corruptus in luxuriam laberetur ac dei praecepta contemneret sicut illi maiores nostri, qui saepe terrenis ac fragilibus his bonis eneruati aberrarunt a disciplina et legis uincla ruperunt. prouidit ergo quatenus cultoribus suis praestaret quietem, si mandata seruassent, et tamen eos emendaret, si praeceptis non obtemperassent. itaque ne tam corrumperentur otio quam patres eorum licentia, premi eos uoluit ab iis in quorum manibus eos conlocauit, ut et labentes confirmet et corruptos ad fortitudinem reparet et fidos experiatur ac temptet. quomodo enim potest imperator militum suorum probare uirtutem, nisi habuerit hostem? et illi tamen aduersarius exsurgit inuito, quia mortalis est et uinci potest, deo autem quia repugnari non potest, ipse aduersarios nomini suo excitat, non qui contra ipsum deum pugnent, sed contra milites eius, ut deuotionem ac fidem suorum uel probet uel conroboret, donec pressurae uerberibus diffluentem corrigat disciplinam.

est et alia causa cur aduersus nos persecutiones fieri sinat, ut dei populus augeatur: nec est difficile monstrare cur aut quomodo id fiat. primum fugantur a deorum cultibus plurimi odio crudelitatis: qui enim talia sacrificia non horreant? deinde placet quibusdam uirtus ac fides ipsa. nonnulli suspicantur deorum cultum non sine causa malum putari a tam multis hominibus, ut emori malint quam id facere quod alii faciunt, ut uiuant. aliquis cupit scire quodnam sit illut bonum quod ad mortem usque defenditur, quod omnibus quae in hac uita iucunda sunt et cara praefertur, a quo nec bonorum nec lucis amissio nec dolor corporis nec uiscerum cruciamenta deterrent. ualent haec plurimum, sed illae maxime causae nostrorum numerum semper auxerunt: audit circumstans populus inter ipsa tormenta dicentes non sacrificare se lapidibus humana manu factis, sed deo uiuo qui sit in caelo. multi hoc uerum esse intellegunt et in pectus admittunt. deinde, ut fieri solet in rebus incertis, dum inter se inuicem quaerant quae sit huius perseuerantiae causa, multa quae ad religionem pertinent diuulgata ac per rumorem uicissim aucupata discuntur: quae quia bona sunt, placeant necesse est. praeterea ultio consecuta, sicut semper accidit, ad credendum uehementer inpellit. ne haec quidem leuis causa est quod inmundi daemonum spiritus accepta licentia multorum se corporibus inmergunt, quibus postea eiectis omnes qui resanati fuerint adhaerent religioni cuius potentiam senserunt. hae tot causae in unum conlatae magnam deo multitudinem mirabiliter adquirunt.

author: Lactantius
english: It is worth knowing their piety, that from the things they do mildly and piously it may be understood what sort of things are done by them against the rights of piety. And lest I seem to attack anyone harshly, I will take for myself some poetic person who is the greatest example of piety. In Maro that king than whom none was more just in piety nor greater in war and arms — what proofs of justice did he put forward for us? He had bound behind their backs the hands of those he would send as offerings to the shades, about to sprinkle the flames with slaughtered blood. What can be milder than this piety … than to sacrifice human victims to the dead and to feed the fire with the blood of humans as with oil? But perhaps this was not his own fault, but the poet's, who stained a man outstanding in piety with an outstanding crime. Where then, O poet, is that piety which you praise so often? See: pious Aeneas seizes four youths born at Sulmo, and as many as Ufens raises, living, to sacrifice them as offerings to the shades and to pour captive blood over the flames of the pyre. Why then was he saying at the very time when he was sending bound humans to immolation, 'I would indeed wish to spare the living also,' when he ordered those living whom he held in his power to be killed in place of cattle? But this, as I said, was not that man's fault, who perhaps had not learned letters, but yours: who, though you were learned, still did not know what piety is, and believed that very thing which he did wickedly and detestably to be the duty of piety; namely he is called pious for this one thing, that he loved his father. What of the fact that good Aeneas slaughtered one praying for things not to be scorned? For though adjured by the same father and the hopes of rising Iulus, he by no means spared, inflamed with furies and anger. Would anyone then think this man had any virtue in himself, who both blazed with fury as with stubble and, forgetful of his father's shades by whom he was asked, could not rein in anger? In no way then pious, who killed not only those not resisting but even those praying.

Someone will say here: what then, or where, or of what sort is piety? Surely with those who do not know wars, who keep concord with all, who are friends even to enemies, who love all humans as brothers, who know how to check anger and to soften every fury of the mind with calm moderation. How great then the darkness, how great the cloud of shadows and errors that has covered human breasts, who when they think themselves most pious then become most impious? For the more religiously they serve these earthly images, the more criminal they stand against the name of true divinity. And so for the merit of their impiety they are often denied by heavier evils: whose cause, because they do not know it, is all ascribed to the fault of fortune, and Epicurus's philosophy finds a place, judging that nothing pertains to the gods and that they are touched neither by favor nor moved by anger, because they often see both their despisers blessed and their worshipers wretched. Which happens because when they seem religious and good by nature, they are believed to deserve nothing such as they often suffer. Yet they console themselves by accusing fortune and do not sense that if there were any, it would never harm its worshipers. Deservedly therefore punishment follows this sort of piety, and offended divinity by the crime of humans wrongly religious slaughters them with heavy misfortune: who though they live with holy manners in highest faith and innocence, yet because they worship gods whose impious and profane rites the true God holds in hatred, are alien from justice and from the name of true piety.

Nor is it hard to teach why worshipers of the gods cannot be good and just. For how will they abstain from blood who worship the bloody gods Mars and Bellona? How will they spare parents who worship Jupiter the expeller of his father, or infants born from themselves who worship Saturn? How will they guard chastity who worship a naked and adulterous goddess and as it were prostituted among the gods? How will they abstain from robberies and frauds who have known the thefts of Mercury teaching that to deceive is not fraud but cleverness? How will they check lusts who venerate Jupiter, Hercules, Liber, Apollo and the rest, whose adulteries and shames against males and females are known not only to the learned but are even expressed in theaters and sung, that they may be more known to all? Can humans be just amid these things, who even if they are good by nature are nevertheless trained to injustice by the gods themselves? For to placate the god you worship you need those things by which you know him to rejoice and be delighted. So it happens that the god shapes the life of the worshipers according to the quality of his own divinity, since the most religious worship is to imitate.

latin: Operae pretium est cognoscere illorum pietatem, ut ex ns quae clementer ac pie faciunt possit intellegi, qualia sint quae ab iis contra iura pietatis geruntur. ac ne quem uidear inclementer incessere, aliquam mihi personam poeticam sumam, quae sit uel maximum pietatis exemplum. aput Maronem rex ille, quo iustior alter nec pietate fuit nec bello maior et armis, quae nobis documenta iustitiae protulit? uinxerat et post terga manus, quos mitteret umbris inferias, caeso sparsurus sanguine flammas. quid potest hac pietate ... clementius, quam mortuis humanas uictimas immolare et ignem cruore hominum tamquam oleo pascere? sed fortasse hoc non ipsius uitium fuerit, sed : poetae, qui insignem pietate uirum insigni scelere foedauerit. ubi est igitur, o poeta, pietas illa quam saepissime laudas? ecce pius Aeneas Sulmone creatos quattuor hic iuuenes, totidem quos educat Ufens, uiuentis rapit, inferias quos immolet umbris captiuoque rogi perfundat sanguine flammas. cur ergo dicebat eodem ipso tempore quo uinctos homines ad immolationem mittebat: equidem et uiuis concedere uellem, cum uiuos quos habebat in potestate uice pecudum iuberet occidi? sed haec, ut dixi, culpa non illius fuit, qui litteras fortasse non didicerat, sed tua: qui cum esses eruditus, ignorasti tamen quid esset pietas, et illut ipsum quod nefarie, quod detestabiliter fecit, pietatis esse officium credidisti; uidelicet ob hoc unum pius uocatur, quod patrem dilexit. quid quod bonus Aeneas haut aspernanda precantis trucidauit? adiuratus enim per eundem patrem et spes surgentis Iuli, nequaquam pepercit furiis accensus et ira. quisquamne igitur hunc putet aliquid in se uirtutis habuisse, qui et furore tamquam stipula exarserit et manium patris per quem rogabatur oblitus iram frenare non quiuerit? nullo igitur modo pius, qui non tantum non repugnantes, sed etiam precantes interemit. dicet hic aliquis: quae ergo aut ubi aut qualis est pietas?*

nimirum aput eos qui bella nesciunt, qui concordiam cum omnibus seruant, qui amici sunt etiam inimicis, qui omnes homines pro fratribus diligunt, qui cohibere iram sciunt omnemque animi furorem tranquilla moderatione lenire. quanta igitur caligo, quanta tenebrarum et errorum nubes hominum pectora obduxit, qui cum se maxime pios putant, tum maxime fiunt inpii? quanto enim religiosius terrenis istis simulacris inseruiunt, tanto magis scelerati aduersus nomen uerae diuinitatis exsistunt. itaque pro merito inpietatis suae grauioribus malis saepe negantur: quorum causam quia nesciunt, fortunae culpa omnis adscribitur, et locum inuenit Epicuri philosophia nihil ad deos pertinere censentis nec gratia eos tangi nec ira moueri, quia et contemptores eorum saepe uideant beatos et cultores saepe miseros. quod eo nt quia cum religiosi uideantur et natura boni, nihil tale creduntur mereri quale saepe patiuntur. consolantur se tamen accusatione fortunae nec sentiunt quod si esset ulla, cultoribus suis numquam noceret. merito igitur huiusmodi pietatem poena consequitur et offensa diuinitas scelere hominum praue religiosorum graui eos infortunio mactat: qui licet sanctis moribus uiuant in summa fide atque innocentia, tamen quia deos colunt, quorum ritus inpios ac profanos deus uerus odio habet, a iustitia et a nomine uerae pietatis alieni sunt. nec est difficile docere cur deorum cultores boni et iusti esse non possint.

quomodo enim sanguine abstinebunt qui colunt cruentos deos Martem atque Bellonam? quomodo aut parentibus parcent qui expulsorem patris sui Iouem aut natis ex se infantibus qui Saturnum? quomodo pudicitiam tuebuntur qui colunt deam nudam et adulteram et quasi aput deos prostitutam? quomodo se rapinis et fraudibus abstinebunt qui Mercuri furta nouerunt docentis non fraudis esse decipere, sed astutiae? quomodo libidines cohercebunt qui Iouem Herculem Liberum Apollinem ceterosque uenerantur, quorum adulteria et stupra in mares et feminas non tantum doctis nota sunt, sed exprimuntur etiam in theatris atque cantantur, ut sint omnibus notiora? possuntne inter haec iusti esse hommes, qui etiamsi natura sint boni, ab ipsis tamen diis erudiantur ad iniustitiam? ad placandum enim deum quem colas iis rebus opus est, quibus illum gaudere ac delectari scias. sic fit ut uitam colentium deus pro qualitate numinis sui formet, quoniam religiosissimus est cultus imitari.

author: Lactantius
english: To those humans, then, who match the manners of their gods: because justice is heavy and bitter, they violently exercise against the just that same impiety which they use in other matters, and not without cause are they named beasts by the prophets. Excellently therefore Marcus Tullius: for if there is no one, he says, who would not rather die than be turned into some shape of a beast, though he would have a human mind, how much more wretched is it to be with a beast-like mind in a human shape? To me it seems so much more, as the mind is more excellent than the body. They therefore scorn the bodies of beasts, than which they themselves are fiercer, and please themselves so much that they were born humans, of whom they bear nothing except the outlines and the outer shape. For what Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania ever fed beasts so savage, so bloodthirsty? Since the rage of all wild animals rages only to the filling of the belly and, when hunger is settled, at once grows quiet. That, that is the true beast, at whose one command black blood is poured everywhere: cruel mourning everywhere, everywhere fear and the fullest image of death. No one can describe for its desert the savagery of this so great beast, which though it lies in one place yet rages through the whole world with iron teeth and not only scatters the limbs of humans but also crushes the bones themselves and rages against the ashes, lest any place of burial remain: as if those who confess God aimed at this, that people should come to their tombs, and not that they themselves should come to God. What savagery, what rage, what madness is that, to have denied light to the living and earth to the dead?

I say therefore that nothing is more wretched than those humans whom necessity either found or made ministers of another's fury, attendants of an impious command. For that was not an honor or advancement of rank, but a human's condemnation to butchery, and God's to everlasting punishment. But what each did through the whole world is impossible to narrate. For what number of volumes will hold such endless, such varied kinds of cruelty? For when power was received each raged according to his own manners. Some from too much fear dared more than they were ordered; others from their own hatred against the just; some from natural fierceness of mind; some, that they might please and by this office pave a way for themselves to higher things; some stood headlong for killing, as one in Phrygia who burned a whole people together with the meeting-place itself. But this one, the fiercer he is, the milder he is found: that worst kind is the one which a false appearance of mildness flatters; that executioner is heavier, fiercer, who has decided to kill no one. And so it cannot be said what great and how heavy kinds of torments judges of this sort invented, that they might reach the effect of their purpose. They do these things not only so that they can boast that they killed none of the innocent — for I myself have heard some boasting that their administration in this part was bloodless — but also for envy, lest either they themselves be conquered or those obtain the glory of their virtue. And so in inventing kinds of punishments they think of nothing else than victory: for they know that that is a contest and a fight. I myself saw in Bithynia a governor wonderfully lifted with joy as if he had subdued some nation of barbarians, because one who had resisted with great virtue for two years at last seemed to yield. They therefore strive to conquer and send sought-out pains into bodies and avoid nothing else than that the tortured not die: as if death alone made people blessed and torments did not, the heavier they are, produce the greater glory of virtue. But they by stubborn folly order care to be applied carefully to the tortured, that the limbs may be renewed for other tortures and new blood be restored for punishment. What so pious, so kind, so humane can be done? They would not have cared so anxiously for those they loved.

This is the teaching of the gods; to these works they train their worshipers; these rites they desire. Moreover the most criminal murderers have founded impious laws against the pious: for both sacrilegious constitutions and unjust disputations of jurists are read. Domitius in the seventh book On the Duty of the Proconsul collected the wicked rescripts of princes, that he might teach with what punishments those ought to be afflicted who confess themselves worshipers of God.

latin: iis igitur hominibus qui deorum suorum moribus congruunt. quia grauis est et acerba iustitia, eandem inpietatem suam qua in ceteris rebus utuntur, aduersus iustos uiolenter exercent, nec inmerito a prophetis bestiae nominantur. praeclare itaque M. Tullius: etenim si nemo est inquit quin emori malit quam conuerti in aliquam figuram bestiae, quamuis hominis mentem sit habiturus, quanto est miserius in hominis figura animo esse efferato? mihi quidem tanto uidetur, quanto praestabilior est animus corpore. aspernantur itaque corpora beluarum, quibus sunt ipsi saeuiores, sibique adeo placent, quod homines nati sint, quorum nihil nisi lineamenta et summam figuram gerunt. nam quis Caucasus, quae India, quae Hyrcania tam inmanes, tam sanguinarias umquam bestias aluit? quoniam ferarum omnium rabies usque ad uentris satietatem furit fameque sedata protinus conquiescit. ilia, illa est uera bestia, cuius una iussione funditur ater ubique cruor: crudelis ubique luctus, ubique pauor et plurima mortis imago . nemo huius tantae beluae inmanitatem potest pro merito describere, quae uno loco recubans tamen per totum orbem ferreis dentibus saeuit et non tantum artus hominum dissipat, sed et ossa ipsa comminuit et in cineres furit, ne quis extet sepulturae locus: quasi uero id adfectent qui deum confitentur; ut ad eorum sepulchra ueniatur, ac non ut ipsi ad deum ueniant. quaenam illa feritas, quae rabies, quae insania est lucem uiuis, terram mortuis denegasse?

dico igitur nihil esse miserius iis hominibus quos ministros furoris alieni, quos satellites inpiae iussionis necessitas aut inuenit aut fecit. non enim honor ille aut prouectio dignitatis fuit, sed hominis damnatio ad carnificinam, dei uero ad poenam sempiternam. quae autem per totum orbem singuli gesserint, enarrare inpossibile est. quis enim uoluminum numerus capiet tam infinita, tam uaria genera crudelitatis V accepta enim potestate pro suis moribus quisque saeuiuit. alii prae nimia timiditate plus ausi sunt quam iubebantur, alii suo proprio aduersus iustos odio, quidam naturali mentis feritate, nonnulli, ut placerent et hoc officio uiam sibi ad altiora munirent; aliqui ad occidendum praecipites extiterunt, sicut unus in Phrygia, qui uniuersum populum cum ipso pariter conuenticulo concremauit. sed hic quanto saeuior, tanto clementior inuenitur: illut uero pessimum genus est cui clementiae species falsa blanditur, ille grauior, ille saeuior est carnifex qui neminem statuit occidere. itaque dici non potest huiusmodi iudices quanta et quam grauia tormentorum genera excogitauerint, ut ad effectum propositi sui peruenirent. haec autem non tantum ideo faciunt, ut gloriari possint nullum se innocentium peremisse — nam et ipse audiui aliquos gloriantes quod administratio sua in hac parte fuerit incruenta —, sed et inuidiae causa, ne aut ipsi uincantur aut illi uirtutis suae gloriam consequantur. itaque in elcogitandis poenarum generibus nihil aliut quam uictoriam cogitant: sciunt enim certamen esse illud et pugnam. uidi ego in Bithynia praesidem gaudio mirabiliter elatum tamquam barbarorum gentem aliquam subegisset, quod unus qui per biennium magna uirtute restiterat, postremo cedere uisus esset. contendunt igitur ut uincant et exquisitos dolores corporibus inmittunt et nihil aliut deuitant quam ut ne torti moriantur: quasi uero mors tantummodo beatos faciat ac non etiam tormenta quanto fuerint grauiora, tanto maiorem uirtutis gloriam pariant. illi autem pertinaci stultitia iubent curam tortis diligenter adhiberi, ut ad alios cruciatus membra renouentur et reparetur nouus sanguis ad poenam. quid tam pium, tam beneficum, tam humanum fieri potest? non curassent tam sollicite quos amarent.

haec est deorum disciplina, ad haec opera cultores suos erudiunt, haec sacra desiderant. quin etiam sceleratissimi homicidae contra pios iura inpia condiderunt: nam et constitutiones sacrilegae et disputationes iuris peritorum leguntur iniustae. Domitius de officio proconsulis libro septimo rescripta principum nefaria collegit, ut doceret quibus poenis adfici oporteret eos qui se cultores dei confiterentur.

author: Lactantius
english: What would you do with those who call 'law' the butcheries of old tyrants raging madly against the innocent? And though they are teachers of injustice and cruelty, they still want to seem just and prudent — blind and dull and ignorant of things and of truth. Is justice so hated by you, O ruined minds, that you equate it with the highest crimes? Has innocence so perished among you that you judge it not even worthy of a simple death, but hold it above all deeds to commit no crime and to keep a heart too little clear of every contagion of crime? And since we speak in common with the worshipers of the gods, let it be allowed through you to do good with you: for this is our law, this work, this religion. If we seem wise to you, imitate; if foolish, scorn or even laugh, if you like: for our folly profits us. Why do you tear? Why do you strike? We do not envy your wisdom: we prefer this folly, we embrace it, we believe this benefits us, that we love you and confer all things on you yourselves who hate.

There is in Cicero a place not far from the truth in that dispute which Furius holds against justice. I ask, he says, if there are two, of whom one is the best man, most equitable, of highest justice, of singular faith, the other of outstanding crime and boldness, and if the city is in this error, that it thinks that good man criminal, wicked, nefarious, and on the contrary judges him who is most wicked to be of highest honesty and faith, and according to this opinion of all citizens that good man is harassed, seized, finally his hands are cut off, his eyes dug out, he is condemned, bound, burned, banished, lacks, and at last by the best right seems to all most wretched, and on the contrary that wicked one is praised, cultivated, loved by all, all honors, all commands, all wealth, all resources from everywhere are conferred on him, and finally he is judged the best man in everyone's estimate and most worthy of every fortune: who at last will be so mad as to doubt which he would rather be? Indeed as if he foresaw what evils and how they would come to us because of justice, he set this example. For our people suffers all these things by the perversity of those who err. See: the city — or rather the whole world itself — is in this error, that it persecutes, tortures, condemns, kills good and just men as if evil and impious.

As for his saying that no one is so mad as to doubt which he would rather be, he indeed, as one who argued against justice, felt this: that the wise man would rather be evil with a good reputation than good with a bad one. But far from us be this madness, that we prefer the false to the true. Will the quality of our good hang on the people's errors rather than on our conscience and God's judgment? Or will any happiness ever entice us so that we would not rather prefer true goodness with every evil than false with every prosperity? Let kings keep their kingdoms for themselves, the rich their riches, as Plautus says, and the prudent their prudence: let them leave us our folly, which even from this appears to be wisdom, that they envy it for us. For who would envy a fool unless he himself were most foolish? But they are not so foolish as to envy fools, but from this, that they persecute carefully and anxiously, they grant that they are not fools. Why else would they rage so cruelly unless they fear that, justice growing stronger day by day, they may be left with their decaying gods? If therefore the worshipers of the gods are wise and we are fools, why do they fear that the wise may be enticed by fools?

latin: Quid iis facias qui ius uocant carnificinas ueterum tyrannorum aduersus innocentes rabide saeuientium? et cum sint iniustitiae crudelitatisque doctores, iustos se tamen ac prudentes uideri uolunt, caeci et hebetes et rerum et ueritatis ignari. adeone uobis, o perditae mentes, inuisa iustitia est, ut eam summis sceleribus adaequetis? adeone. aput uos perit innocentia, ut ne morte quidem simplici dignam iudicetis, sed supra omnia facinora habeatur nullum facinus admittere pectusque parum ab omni sceleris contagione praestare? et quoniam communiter cum deorum cultoribus loquimur, liceat per uos bene facere uobiscum: haec est enim lex nostra, hoc opus, haec religio. si uobis sapientes uidemur, imitamini, si stulti, contemnite aut etiam ridete, si libet: nobis enim stultitia nostra prodest. quid laceratis? quid adfligitis? non inuidemus sapientiae uestrae: hanc stultitiam malumus, hanc amplectimur, hoc nobis credimus expedire, ut uos diligamus et in uos ipsos qui odistis omnia conferamus.

est apud Ciceronem non abhorrens a uero locus in ea disputatione quae habetur a Furio contra iustitiam. quaero inquit, si duo sint, quorum alter. optimus uir, aequissimus, summa iustitia, singulari fide, alter insigni scelere et audacia, et si in eo sit errore ciuitas, ut bonum illum uirum sceleratum facinerosum nefarium putet, contra autem (eum) qui sit inprobis simus, elxistimet esse summa probitate ac fide, proque hac opinione omnium ciuium bonus ille uir uexetur rapiatur, manus ei denique auferantur, effodiantur oculi, damnetur uinciatur uratur exterminetur egeat, postremo iure etiam optimo omnibus miserrimus esse uideatur, contra autem ille inprobus laudetur colatur, ab omnibus diligatur, omnes ad eum honores, omnia imperia, omnes opes, omnes undique copiae conferantur, uir denique optimus omnium existimatione et dignissimus omni fortuna iudicetur: quis tandem erit tam demens qui dubitet utrum se esse malit? profecto quasi diuinaret quae nobis mala et quo modo euentura essent propter iustitiam, hoc posuit exemplum. haec enim populus noster patitur omnia errantium prauitate. ecce in eo est errore ciuitas uel potius orbis ipse totus, ut bonos et iustos uiros tamquam malos et impios persequatur excruciet damnet occidat. nam quod ait neminem esse tam dementem qui dubitet utrum se esse malit, ille quidem ut is qui contra iustitiam disserebat, hoc sensit, malle sapientem malum esse cum bona existimatione quam bonum cum mala.

a nobis autem absit haec amentia, ut falsum uero anteponamus. an boni nostri qualitas ex populi pendebit erroribus quam ex conscientia nostra et iudicio dei? aut aliqua nos felicitas inliciet umquam, ut non potius ueram bonitatem cum omni malo quam falsam cum omni prosperitate malimus? sua sibi habeant regna reges, suas diuitias diuites, ut loquitur Plautus, suam uero prudentiam prudentes: relinquant nobis stultitiam nostram, quam uel ex hoc apparet esse sapientiam quod eam nobis inuident. quis enim stulto inuideat nisi qui ipse sit stultissimus? illi autem non sunt adeo stulti ut stultis inuideant, sed ex eo quod accurate, quod sollicite persecuntur, stultos non esse concedunt. cur enim tam crudeliter saeuiant nisi quia metuunt, ne in dies inualescente iustitia cum diis suis cariosis relinquantur? si ergo cultores deorum sapientes sunt et nos stulti, quid metuant ne sapientes inliciantur a stultis?

author: Lactantius
english: I have set out why the philosophers could neither find justice nor defend it: now I return to what I had aimed at. Carneades therefore, since what the philosophers asserted was weak, took boldness to refute, because he understood it could be refuted. The sum of his dispute was this: that humans sanctioned laws for themselves for utility, namely varied according to customs, and among the same people often changed according to times, but that there is no natural right; that all both humans and other animals are driven to their own advantages with nature leading; accordingly that justice is either nothing or, if there is any, it is the height of folly, since it would harm itself by consulting others' benefits. And he brought in these arguments: that for all peoples who flourished by empire and for the Romans themselves also, who possessed the whole world, if they should wish to be just, that is if they restore what is another's, they must return to huts and lie in want and miseries. Then leaving common matters he came to particular ones.

A good man, he says, if he has a runaway slave or an unhealthy and plague-ridden house, whose faults he alone knows, and therefore advertises them to sell, will he declare that he is selling a runaway slave or a plague-ridden house, or will he hide it from the buyer? If he declares, he will be judged good indeed, because he will not deceive, but still foolish, because he will either sell cheaply or not sell at all; if he hides, he will be wise indeed, because he will consult his interest, but the same man wicked, because he will deceive. Again if he finds someone who thinks he is selling brass, when it is gold, or lead, when it is silver, will he be silent, to buy it cheap, or will he point it out, to buy dear? It plainly seems foolish to prefer to buy dear. From which he wanted it understood both that he who is just and good is foolish and that he who is wise is wicked, and yet that it can happen without ruin that humans be content with poverty. He therefore crossed to greater matters, in which no one could be just without danger to life.

For he said: surely justice is not to kill a human, not to touch what is another's at all. What then will the just man do if by chance he has suffered shipwreck and someone weaker in strength has seized a plank? Will he not thrust that man from the plank, so that he himself may climb and escape by leaning on it, especially when there is no witness in mid-sea? If he is wise, he will do it: for he himself must perish unless he does it; but if he prefers to die rather than lay hands on another, then that man is just, but (the same) foolish, who does not spare his own life while he spares another's. Likewise if when his own battle-line is routed the enemies begin to pursue, and that just man has found someone wounded sitting on a horse, will he spare him, so that he himself may be killed, or throw him from the horse, so that he himself can flee the enemy? If he does it, he is wise, but the same wicked; if he does not, he must be just, but the same foolish. So then when he had divided justice into two parts, saying one is civic, the other natural, he overturned both, because that civic one is wisdom indeed, but is not justice, while that natural one is justice indeed, but is not wisdom. These things are plainly sharp and poisoned and such as Marcus Tullius could not refute. For when he makes Laelius answer Furius and speak for justice, he passed by these things unrefuted as if past a pit, so that the same Laelius seems to have defended not the natural justice, which had come under the charge of folly, but that civic justice, which Furius had granted was wisdom indeed, but unjust.

latin: Exposui causam cur philosophi nec inuenire iustitiam nec defendere potuerunt: nunc redeo ad id quod intenderam. tarneades ergo, quoniam erant mfirma quae a philosophis adserebantur, sumpsit audaciam refellendi, quia refelli posse intellexit. eius disputationis summa haec fuit: iura sibi homines pro utilitate sanxisse, scilicet uaria pro moribus, et aput eosdem pro temporibus saepe mutata, ius autem naturale esse nullum; omnes et homines et alias animantes ad utilitates suas natura ducente ferri; proinde aut nullam esse iustitiam aut, si sit aliqua, summam esse stultitiam, quoniam sibi noceret alienis commodis consulens. et inferebat haec argumenta: omnibus populis qui florerent inperio et Romanis quoque ipsis, qui totius orbis potirentur, si iusti uelint esse, hoc est si aliena restituant, ad casas esse redeundum et in egestate ac miseriis iacendum. tum omissis communibus ad propria ueniebat.

bonus uir inquit si habeat seruum fugitiuum uel domum insalubrem ac pestilentem, quae uitia solus sciat, et ideo proscribat ut uendat, utrumne profitebitur fugitiuum se seruum uel pestilentem domum uendere an celabit emptorem? si profitebitur, bonus quidem, quia non fallet, sed tamen stultus iudicabitur, quia uel paruo uendet uel omnino non uendet; si celabit, erit quidem sapiens, quia rei consulet, sed idem malus, quia fallet. rursus si reperiat aliquem qui orichalcum se putet uendere, cum sit illut aurum, aut plumbum, cum sit argentum, tacebitne, ut id paruo emat, an indicabit, ut magno? stultum plane uidetur malle magno. unde intellegi uolebat et eum qui sit iustus ac bonus stultum esse et eum qui sapiens, malum, et tamen sine pernicie fieri posse ut sint homines paupertate contenti. transcendebat ergo ad maiora, m quibus nemo posset sine periculo uitae iustus esse.

dicebat enim: nempe iustitia est hominem non occidere, alienum prorsus non attingere. quid ergo iustus faciet, si forte naufragium fecerit et aliquis inbecillior uiribus tabu lam ceperit? nonne illum tabula deturbabit, ut ipse conscendat eaque nixus euadat, maxime cum sit nullus medio mari testis? si sapiens est, faciet: ipsi enim pereundum est, nisi fecerit; si autem mori maluerit quam manus inferre alteri, iam iustus ille, sed (idem) stultus est, qui uitae suae non parcat, dum parcit alienae. item si acie suorum fusa hostes insequi coeperint, et iustus ille nanctus fuerit aliquem saucium equo insidentem, eine parcet, ut ipse occidatur, an deiciet ex equo, ut ipse hostem possit effugere? quod si fecerit, sapiens, sed idem malus, si non fecerit, iustus, sed idem stultus sit necesse est. ita ergo iustitiam cum in duas partes diuisisset, alteram ciuilem esse dicens, alteram naturalem, utramque subuertit, quod illa ciuilis sapientia sit quidem, sed iustitia non sit, naturalis autem illa iustitia sit quidem, sed non sit sapientia. arguta haec plane ac uenenata sunt et quae Marcus Tullius non potuerit refellere. nam cum faciat Laelium Furio respondentem pro iustitiaque dicentem, inrefutata haec tamquam foueam praetergressus est, ut uideatur idem Laelius non naturalem, quae in crimen stultitiae uenerat, sed illam ciuilem defendisse iustitiam, quam Furius sapientiam quidem esse concesserat, sed iniustam.

author: Lactantius
english: What belonged to the present dispute I have shown: how justice bears a likeness of folly, that it may appear they are not deceived without cause who think the people of our religion fools, who seem to do such things as that man proposed. Now I sense a greater thing is demanded of me: that I show why God willed to wrap justice in the appearance of folly and take it from human eyes, if I first answer Furius, because Laelius answered too little fully. He indeed, though he was wise as he was called, still could by no means patronize true justice, because he did not hold the head itself and fountain of justice. For us that defense is easier, to whom by heavenly benefit justice is familiar and inwardly known, and who know it not by name but by the thing. For Plato and Aristotle wished with honest will to defend justice and would have effected something if the teaching of divine things also had helped their good attempts, their eloquence, the virtue of their talent. And so that work of theirs lay empty and useless and could persuade no human to live by their prescription, because that discipline did not have a foundation from heaven. Our work must be more certain, whom God has taught. For they painted with words and imagined a justice that was not in sight, nor could they confirm by present examples what they asserted. For hearers could answer that one cannot live as they prescribed by their dispute, so much so that none have yet appeared who followed that kind of life. But we show not by words only but also by examples drawn from the true that what is said by us is true. Carneades therefore sensed what the nature of justice is, except that he did not look deep enough that folly is not... although I seem to myself to understand with what mind he did that. For he did not truly think him a fool who is just, but when he knew he was not and yet did not grasp the reason why he seemed so, he wanted to show that truth lies hidden, that he might guard the decree of his school, whose chief sentence is that nothing can be perceived. Let us see then whether justice can have some treaty with folly.

Is justice then, O Furius or rather O Carneades whose is that whole speech, so empty, so superfluous and so contemptible to God that it can do nothing and have nothing in itself that avails for its own guard? But clearly those who are ignorant of the human's sacrament and therefore refer all things to this temporal life cannot know how great the force of justice is. For even when they dispute about virtue, though they understand it is fullest of hardships and miseries, still they say it is to be sought for its own sake: for they by no means see its rewards, which are eternal and immortal. So by referring all things to this present life they plainly reduce virtue to folly, if indeed it takes up such great labors of this life in vain and emptily — but these things more fully in another place; meanwhile about justice, as we began: whose force is so great that when it has lifted eyes to heaven it merits all things from God. Rightly therefore Flaccus said the force of innocence is so great that for its own protection it needs neither arms nor strength wherever it journeys: 'The man upright in life and pure of crime needs no Moorish javelins nor bow nor quiver heavy with poisoned arrows, Fuscus, whether about to journey through the hot Syrtes or through the inhospitable Caucasus or the places the storied Hydaspes washes.' It cannot therefore happen that heavenly guardianship not keep the just human among the dangers of storms and wars and that, even if he sail with parricides and the guilty, either the wicked also be spared that one just and innocent soul may be freed, or at least when the rest perish he alone be saved. But let us grant that what the philosopher proposes can happen: what then will the just man do if he has found either a wounded man on a horse or a shipwrecked man on a plank? Not unwillingly I confess: he will die rather than kill. Nor therefore will justice, which is the singular good of a human, take the name of folly. For what better, what dearer ought a human to have than innocence? Which must be so much more perfect as you lead it to the extreme and prefer to die, lest anything be diminished from the account of innocence. It is folly, he says, to spare another's soul with ruin of one's own. Will you also judge it foolish to perish for friendship? Why then are those Pythagorean comrades praised by you, of whom one gave himself to the tyrant as surety of death for the other, and the other at the set time, when already his guarantor was being led, made his own presence and freed him by his intervention? Whose virtue would not be held in such glory — that one willed to die for a friend, the other even for faith — if they were thought fools. Finally for this very virtue the tyrant returned them favor by saving both and the nature of a most cruel human was changed. Indeed he is even said to have begged that they receive him as a third into friendship, not surely as fools but as good and wise men. And so I do not see why, when to die for friendship and faith is counted highest glory, it should not also be glorious for a human to perish for innocence.

Therefore most foolish are those who charge us as a crime with willing to die for God, when they themselves lift to heaven with highest praises him who willed to die for a human. Finally, to conclude the dispute, reason itself teaches that the same man cannot be just and foolish, the same wise and unjust. For he who is foolish does not know what is just and good and therefore always sins. For he is led as a captive by vices and can by no means resist, because he lacks virtue, which he does not know. But the just man abstains from every sin, which he cannot otherwise do than if he has knowledge of right and wrong. Who can discern the right from the wrong unless the wise man? So it happens that he who is foolish can never be just, nor he wise who has been unjust. And if this is most true, it is clear that he who has not taken the plank from the shipwrecked or the horse from the wounded is not foolish, because to do these things is sin, from which the wise man abstains. Yet I myself confess that he also seems so through the error of humans ignorant of each thing's property. And so this whole question is dissolved not so much by arguments as by definition. Folly therefore is a wandering in deeds and words through ignorance of the right and good. Therefore he is not a fool who does not spare even himself, provided he not harm another, which is evil. Which indeed reason and truth itself prescribe for us. For in all animals we see that, because they lack wisdom, nature is the reconciler of itself. They therefore harm others, that they may profit themselves: for they do not know that it is evil to harm. But a human, because he has knowledge of good and evil, abstains from harming even with his own inconvenience, which an irrational animal cannot do, and therefore among a human's highest virtues innocence is counted. By which things it appears that he is most wise who prefers to perish lest he harm, that he may keep that duty by which he is distinguished from the mute. For he who does not refute a seller's error, that he may buy gold cheap, or who does not declare that he sells a runaway slave or a pestilent house, consulting his gain and convenience, is not that wise man as Carneades wished him to seem, but cunning and crafty. But cunning and craftiness are in mute animals also, either when they ambush others and take them by deceit to devour them, or when they mock others' ambushes by various kinds; but wisdom falls to the human alone. For wisdom is understanding either for doing the good and right or for abstinence from wicked words and deeds. But a wise man never aims at gain, because he despises these earthly goods, nor does he suffer anyone to be deceived, because it is a good man's duty to correct humans' errors and lead them back into the way, since a human's nature is social and beneficent, by which alone he has kinship with God.
